prize_parts.citation: for a body of work that renews lyric, narrative and the essay through a sustained, inventive dialogue with antiquity, joining scholarly exactness to formal daring and emotional force

statement.case_for: After the exchange and the chair's questions, my configuration is unchanged: Carson as sole laureate. The reasons have become more specific. The chair asked whether a Carson citation can be confined to original written work. I think it can, and that narrowing improves the case. Autobiography of Red is a verse novel in which myth, the line and the narrative arc pull against one another. Nox is an elegy for a brother that works through a translation of Catullus, glosses and fragments, and its language carries the grief. I take both from public description and not from verified reading. Beyond these two books, my understanding of the wider oeuvre is that the essays in Eros the Bittersweet and Glass, Irony and God, the prose-poem and lyric collections of the 1990s and 2000s such as Short Talks, Plainwater and Men in the Off Hours, The Beauty of the Husband, and the later Red Doc> and Float show one intelligence moving between forms. Whether all of these reach the level of the two landmark books I cannot say with confidence, and I do not ask the committee to rely on my impression. The central claim is a voice that is exact, cool and sometimes comic, and that turns suddenly to desire or loss, together with an intellectual depth that comes from long work on Greek and Latin literature. The method is not decorative, because the scholarship and the feeling are not separable in the best books. She writes in English, so I can judge the language directly. I treat that as a reduction of uncertainty and not as an argument for merit. It also means my confidence in her may be inflated relative to translated writers, as Swärd noted. I have therefore tried to hold the other candidates to the same criteria and not to the standard of what I can read unaided.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation remains sustained quality across the whole corpus. The reputation does concentrate in a few books, much of the output is deliberately occasional, fragmentary or dependent on physical form, and translations, adaptations and scholarship sit uneasily beside original creation. If the committee examined the mid-career and later books and found them uneven, or judged the hybrid mode peripheral to Nobel's will, then Cărtărescu's long single project would have the stronger claim to maturity. Robinson's compact, coherent fiction would be a different kind of challenge. On the other side, Mattson and Sem-Sandberg have not been shown that Cărtărescu's recurring imagery is development and not repetition, and neither has anyone shown the reverse. That open question cuts against both leading candidates. It does not settle the matter in favor of Carson. It leaves her case with a risk I would not minimize.

responses.point: Olsson asked me directly whether the essays are strong enough to bear weight in a citation. He also summarized my position as ranking Robinson third for a restrained, morally serious prose with a compact fiction corpus, and as saying that Carson's translations and essays are hard to weigh against the original work.
responses.response: On the essays, my answer is a measured yes. As I understand them, they are works of criticism that are also literary writing, since argument, image and sentence-level style cannot be separated in them. They deserve to be named in the citation as one of the three forms renewed, alongside lyric and narrative. I would not make them carry the claim alone, and I cannot verify every volume. That does not widen the scope to translation. The essays are original prose, and the translations remain context. As for Robinson, I would put my own position slightly differently from his summary. In round 1 I listed her as a third alternative because a compact and consistent corpus makes a serious claim to sustained quality. I did not rank her above Carson. I accept his point that the breadth of her significance is less settled, and it is the reason she stays a distant alternative for me.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says he is more confident that the literary claim for Cărtărescu can be stated as a claim about language and construction on the page. He doubts that Carson's book-object and translation work can be folded into the achievement without cost, and he says he cannot judge the material dimension of Nox from description.
responses.response: I think the chair's first question is aimed at exactly this objection. If the citation names only the verse novel, the lyric, the elegiac writing and the essays, the material dimension of Nox drops out of the credited claim. What remains is a claim about language and construction on the page, which is the form of claim he finds more secure for Cărtărescu. Nox would still count as evidence of her method, but it would not carry the prize. I hope that answers his objection about scope. It does not answer his other question, about the durability of the later work, and I concede that. I also take his point that agreement between supporters is not evidence. I am not weighing the number of colleagues who share my first choice. My difference with him is about which risk is smaller: unevenness across Carson's varied books, or repetition inside Cărtărescu's single large project. I hold my view with real uncertainty, and he may be right that the second is the lesser risk.

responses.point: Mattson argues that, if Carson's standing depends on a handful of landmark books, the sustained-quality criterion favors a writer whose whole body of work shows one developing project. She accepts that her own worry about repetition in Cărtărescu is the main uncertainty in her ranking.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my preference, and I do not think it can be dismissed. A coherent long project is a recognizable form of maturity. My disagreement is about what counts as development. Carson's recurring ground of antiquity, desire and grief is treated through changing instruments: verse novel, elegy, essay, tango sequence. I read that change of method as a sign that the work keeps discovering form, which she would call development. That reading rests on public knowledge and not on a full corpus check, and the landmark-books worry applies to it. Her own admission that she cannot verify whether the recurrences in the late Cărtărescu volumes are structural is the same limit that I face with Carson's mid-career books. I therefore do not read her ranking as a weak one. I read the dispute as narrow, and I still end on the side of Carson.

responses.point: Swärd flags that she can judge Carson's English more directly than translated writers, and that this asymmetry may inflate her confidence in Carson. She also says the citation should rest on the books that carry the achievement and not claim every occasional piece.
responses.response: I share both points. The asymmetry affects me as well, and one concrete way I try to correct for it is to refuse to let directness of access count as literary merit. I treat it only as fewer unknowns in the assessment. Her second point is why I keep my citation short and name forms and a relation to antiquity, without listing titles or claiming every decade. I would add that this is a reason to prefer an oeuvre-level citation. A citation naming a single mode of work would be easier to defend in the committee and harder to defend against the evidence.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified the corpus. My knowledge of Carson's mid-career, later, shorter and performance works is uneven, and the claim that they sustain the quality of Autobiography of Red and Nox remains untested.

How to weigh translations, adaptations and scholarship against her original poetry and prose in one citation is unresolved. I would resolve it by crediting only the original written work, but the committee may judge that scope too narrow or too wide.
The physical and visual form of Nox cannot be conveyed by public summaries. Sem-Sandberg's concern about judging it from description applies to me as well.
Whether the hybrid practice is read as a core literary achievement within the framework of Nobel's will is a matter of committee judgment and is not settled by public information.

For Cărtărescu and Adonis, the effects of the original Romanian and Arabic reach me only through translation. Whether his recurring imagery is development or repetition is not something I can settle, and the same limit applies to my colleagues.
The preference for Carson over Cărtărescu is narrow. A comparison of specific volumes, or an expert reading of the originals, could change it.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. Documented connections are co-election to the Academy with David Håkansson, collaboration with Kate Larson, work on Selma Lagerlöf, and service with committee colleagues. None is a documented link to a shortlisted writer. My own practice as a novelist, short-story writer and biographer is context and not evidence of preference. I disclose that I am one of the four explicit B002 supporters named in the chair's summary. That count depends partly on the modeled vote of the co-opted member Carlberg, and I do not treat it as literary merit. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
